question: Aspirated foreign bodies preferentially enter the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter, and more vertically oriented (less angled from the tracheal axis) than the left main bronchus, making it the more direct continuation of the trachea.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical (smaller angle from trachea ~25–30°) compared to the left (~45–55°). Foreign bodies therefore preferentially enter the right main bronchus, most commonly lodging in the right lower lobe bronchus. This anatomical fact explains why right-sided obstructive emphysema or collapse is the more common radiological finding.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and takes off at a smaller angle from the trachea (approximately 25–30° vs 45–55° for the left) — making it the anatomical 'fast lane' for any aspirated material. This predisposition is even more pronounced in children due to the relatively symmetrical tracheal bifurcation at younger ages, but the right bronchus remains the more likely destination.
